prompt: Worst-case time to search a balanced BST of n nodes?
explain: Each comparison discards half the remaining subtree.

prompt: Which traversal of a BST visits keys in sorted order?
explain: Left subtree, node, right subtree - ascending by construction.

prompt: Time to read element i of an array?
explain: The address is base + i x stride, so the index is arithmetic rather than search.

prompt: Worst-case time for linear search over n items?
explain: The target may be last, or absent, so every item is touched.

prompt: Binary search requires the input to be what?
explain: Without order there is no way to know which half to discard.

prompt: A stack removes items in which order?
explain: Push and pop both act on the same end.

prompt: A queue removes items from which end?
explain: Enqueue at the back, dequeue at the front - first in, first out.

prompt: Time to insert at the head of a singly linked list?
explain: One new node, one pointer rewrite. No shifting, unlike an array.

prompt: Time to reach the middle element of a singly linked list?
explain: There is no indexing - you walk from the head, which is the price of cheap insertion.

prompt: Space for an adjacency matrix on V vertices?
explain: A full V by V grid, whether or not the graph is sparse.

prompt: Worst-case time for merge sort?
explain: log n levels of splitting, n work merging at each level - and no bad input changes that.

prompt: Which of these sorts is stable?
explain: Merge sort breaks ties toward the left run. The other three can reorder equal keys.

prompt: How many edges does a tree with n nodes have?
explain: Every node but the root contributes exactly one edge to its parent.

prompt: Depth-first search is naturally written with which structure?
explain: Recursion is a stack too - the call stack is doing the work.

prompt: Breadth-first search is written with which structure?
explain: Finish one layer before starting the next, which is first in, first out.

prompt: Average-case time for a hash table lookup?
explain: Average, not worst. A bad hash or a full table degrades it.

prompt: Height of a complete binary tree with n nodes?
explain: Each level roughly doubles the node count, so depth grows logarithmically.

prompt: Best-case time for bubble sort with early exit?
explain: One clean pass over sorted input swaps nothing, so it stops.

prompt: What does a max-heap guarantee about its root?
explain: The heap property is local - parent beats child - and that makes the root the global maximum.

prompt: Time to append to a dynamic array, amortised?
explain: Doubling makes the occasional copy rare enough to average out to constant.

prompt: Time to build a heap from an unsorted array of n items?
explain: Sift down from the middle: the level sizes form a converging series, so it is linear, not n log n.

prompt: Worst-case time for quicksort?
explain: A pivot that splits off one element each time gives n levels of n work.

prompt: Extra space used by heapsort?
explain: The heap is built inside the array being sorted, which is its advantage over merge sort.

prompt: Auxiliary space for standard array merge sort?
explain: Merging needs somewhere to write the combined run.

prompt: Worst-case time for a hash table lookup?
explain: If every key collides, the bucket is a list and you walk all of it.

prompt: Dijkstra with a binary heap runs in?
explain: Each edge may push a key, and each pop costs log V. Often written O(E log V).

prompt: Which shortest-path algorithm breaks on negative edge weights?
explain: Dijkstra finalises a node on pop, and a later negative edge could have improved it.

prompt: Bellman-Ford on V vertices and E edges runs in?
explain: V-1 relaxation rounds, every edge each round.

prompt: Which structure does Kruskal use to reject cycle-forming edges?
explain: Two endpoints already in one set means the edge would close a cycle.

prompt: What dominates Kruskal's running time?
explain: E log E to sort, against almost-constant union-find per edge.

prompt: Shortest path in an unweighted graph is found by?
explain: Equal edge costs mean layer order is distance order, so BFS is enough.

prompt: Topological sorting is possible only on what kind of graph?
explain: A cycle has no valid first element, so no ordering exists.

prompt: Extra space to reverse a singly linked list in place?
explain: Three pointers walked along the list - previous, current, next.

prompt: Counting sort over n items with key range k runs in?
explain: One pass to tally, one over the range to emit. Useless when k dwarfs n.

prompt: Looking up a word of length m in a trie costs?
explain: One step per character, independent of how many words the trie holds.

prompt: Worst-case recursion depth of DFS on V vertices?
explain: A path graph forces the stack to the full length - which is how DFS blows the stack.

prompt: Deleting the minimum from a binary min-heap costs?
explain: Reading it is constant, but restoring the heap sifts down one full height.

prompt: Finding the minimum in a max-heap of n items costs?
explain: The heap property says nothing about the smallest, and it is in some leaf - so you scan them all.

prompt: An unbalanced BST built from sorted input degrades search to?
explain: Each insert goes right, so the tree is a linked list wearing a tree's clothes.

prompt: Two-pointer scanning on a sorted array typically costs?
explain: Each pointer only moves forward, so together they take at most n steps.

prompt: Floyd-Warshall on V vertices runs in?
explain: Three nested loops - every pair, tried through every intermediate.

prompt: Amortised cost per union-find operation with path compression and union by rank?
explain: O(alpha(n)), which is under 5 for any n you will ever store - constant in practice but not in theory.

prompt: KMP preprocessing on a pattern of length m costs?
explain: The failure table is built in one pass with the same two-pointer trick as the search.

prompt: Optimal time to find the median of two sorted arrays of sizes m and n?
explain: Binary search the split point in the shorter array rather than merging.

prompt: Longest common subsequence of lengths m and n by DP costs?
explain: One cell per prefix pair, each filled in constant time.

prompt: 0/1 knapsack DP with n items and capacity W costs?
explain: A table of items by capacities. Pseudo-polynomial: W is exponential in its own bit length.

prompt: Why is the knapsack DP called pseudo-polynomial?
answer: W is exponential in the bits used to write it
choices: W is exponential in the bits used to write it
it is only polynomial on average
it only works for small n
explain: Input size counts digits. W written in binary takes log W bits, so O(nW) is exponential in the real input length.

prompt: Tarjan's strongly connected components algorithm runs in?
explain: A single DFS with low-link values - no second pass needed, unlike Kosaraju's two.

prompt: A range query on a segment tree over n elements costs?
explain: Any range decomposes into at most two nodes per level of the tree.

prompt: A point update on a Fenwick tree costs?
explain: You walk up by adding the lowest set bit, which happens log n times.

prompt: A* returns an optimal path when its heuristic is?
explain: Overestimating can prune the true best path. Underestimating only costs you extra exploration.

prompt: Edmonds-Karp maximum flow runs in?
explain: BFS augmenting paths bound the number of rounds at O(VE), each costing O(E).

prompt: Matrix chain multiplication by DP over n matrices costs?
explain: O(n^2) subchains, each trying O(n) split points.

prompt: Which algorithm finds the k-th smallest element in expected linear time?
explain: Partition like quicksort, then recurse into one side only - n + n/2 + n/4 converges to 2n.

prompt: Extra space used by the Boyer-Moore majority vote algorithm?
explain: One candidate and one counter, in a single pass.

prompt: Building a suffix array by prefix doubling costs?
explain: log n doubling rounds, each sorting ranks in linear time with radix sort.

prompt: Which of these decision problems is NP-complete?
choices: single-source shortest path with non-negative weights
explain: The other three have known polynomial algorithms - Dijkstra, Kruskal, and Hopcroft-Karp.

prompt: Why can memoised recursion still blow up where bottom-up DP does not?
answer: the recursion depth itself can exceed the stack
choices: the recursion depth itself can exceed the stack
memoisation does not reduce the work
explain: Same asymptotic work, but a chain of n nested calls needs n stack frames that a loop never allocates.
